en: Dīgha Nikāya 4:
The Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta 1.
The Brahmin Householders of Campā
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Aṅgas with a large Saṅgha of about five hundred bhikkhus, arrived at Campā.
There the Blessed One stayed near Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond.

Now at that time, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa was residing in Campā—a city teeming with living beings, abundant in grass, timber, water, and grain, a royal domain granted as a royal gift and a brahminical endowment by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
The brahmin householders of Campā heard:
"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, while wandering on tour among the Aṅgas, [accompanied] by a great..."
Together with a community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, he arrived at Campā and was staying there on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond.
Now, this excellent report of the venerable Gotama’s fame has spread abroad:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having personally realized this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—through direct higher knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life in its entirety, perfectly pure.
“It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Campā, departing from Campā in groups and crowds, approached the Gaggarā Lotus Pond.
At that time, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa had retired to the upper terrace for his midday rest.
The brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa saw the brahmin householders of Campā leaving Campā in large groups and crowds, heading toward the Gaggarā lotus pond.
Seeing them, he addressed his steward:
“Why, sir steward, are the brahmin householders of Campā leaving Campā in large groups and crowds, heading toward the Gaggarā lotus pond?”
“Sir, there is indeed a recluse named Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan; while wandering on tour among the Aṅgas with a great community of monks,
numbering about five hundred monks, he has arrived at Campā and is staying at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond.”
“Furthermore, this good report has spread concerning the venerable Gotama:

‘Truly, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
It is for the sake of seeing that venerable Gotama that they are approaching him.”
“In that case, good steward, go to where the brahmin householders of Campā are and, having approached them, say this to the brahmin householders of Campā:
‘Gentlemen, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa says:
“May you please wait; the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa will also go to see the ascetic Gotama.”’”
“Yes, sir,” the steward replied to the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa. He then approached the brahmin householders of Campā and, having approached them, said this to the brahmin householders of Campā:
“Sirs, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa says this:
‘May you please wait, for the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa will also go to see the ascetic Gotama.’”
2. The Discourse on the Qualities of Soṇadaṇḍa.
Now at that time, about five hundred brahmins from various kingdoms were staying in Campā for some business or other.
Those brahmins heard:
“It is said that the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa will approach the ascetic Gotama to see him.
Then those brahmins went to where the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa was, and having approached him, they said this to the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa:
“Is it true, sir, that you, Soṇadaṇḍa, will approach the ascetic Gotama to see him?”
“Indeed, sir, this is my thought:
‘I too shall go to see the ascetic Gotama.
“Do not, Master Soṇadaṇḍa, go to see the ascetic Gotama.”
It is not fitting for Master Soṇadaṇḍa to go to see the ascetic Gotama.
If Master Soṇadaṇḍa were to go to see the ascetic Gotama, Master Soṇadaṇḍa’s reputation would diminish, while the ascetic Gotama’s reputation would increase.
Since Master Soṇadaṇḍa’s reputation would diminish and the ascetic Gotama’s reputation would increase, on this account it is not fitting for Master Soṇadaṇḍa to go to see the ascetic Gotama.
The ascetic Gotama, however, ought to come to visit the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa.
For the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent as far back as the seventh generation of ancestors, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth.
Furthermore, that the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent...
For seven generations back, we have been unassailable and beyond reproach regarding our birth; in this respect,
Master Soṇadaṇḍa does not deserve to approach the ascetic Gotama for an audience,
but rather the ascetic Gotama deserves to approach Master Soṇadaṇḍa for an audience.
For Master Soṇadaṇḍa is wealthy, of great fortune, and of great possessions...

[as before] ...Master Soṇadaṇḍa is a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas together with their glossaries (nighaṇṭu) and liturgical formulas (keṭubha), including phonology (sakkharappabheda) and etymology as the fifth, a master of word-analysis and grammar, and one who is well-versed in Lokāyata philosophy and the marks of a Great Man... [as before] ...

For Master Soṇadaṇḍa is handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring; he is endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, possessing a divine form and a divine grace, and is of no mean appearance to look upon...
[as before] ...For Master Soṇadaṇḍa is virtuous, possessed of the virtue of the elders, and endowed with the virtue of the elders...

[as before] ...For Master Soṇadaṇḍa is a man of beautiful speech, with a beautiful delivery, endowed with speech that is polished, distinct, free from indistinctness, and capable of making the meaning known... [as before] ...
For Master Soṇadaṇḍa is the teacher of many teachers; he teaches the mantras to three hundred young brahmins.
Indeed, many young brahmins come from various directions and various countries into the presence of Master Soṇadaṇḍa, seeking the mantras and desiring to master them... [and so forth].
For Master Soṇadaṇḍa is old, aged, advanced in years, come to the end of his life’s span, and has reached the final stage of existence;
whereas the ascetic Gotama is young and a recent renunciant...
[as above] ...Moreover, Master Soṇadaṇḍa is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha... [as above] ...
For Master Soṇadaṇḍa is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by the brahmin Pokkharasāti...

[and so on] ...For Master Soṇadaṇḍa presides over Campā, which is populous, abounding in grass, timber, water, and grain; it is a royal domain, a royal gift granted by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, a royal endowment for the benefit of brahmins.

“Furthermore, since Master Soṇadaṇḍa dwells in Campā— a city teeming with people, abundant in grass, timber, water, and grain, a royal domain granted as a brahmin gift by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha—
for this reason also, Master Soṇadaṇḍa does not deserve to approach the ascetic Gotama for an audience; rather,
it is the ascetic Gotama who deserves to approach Master Soṇadaṇḍa for an audience.”
3. Discourse on the Qualities of the Buddha.
When this was said, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa said this to those brahmins:
"In that case, sirs, listen to me as well, as to how we ourselves are worthy to approach that Blessed One Gotama for a visit."
But it is not fitting that the venerable Gotama should come to see us.

For the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent for seven generations back, unassailable and beyond reproach in regard to his birth.
Moreover, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent...
We are seven generations back from our grandfather’s generation, unaccused and irreproachable in matters of birth; in this respect,
that venerable Gotama does not deserve to come to see us,
but rather we ourselves ought to go to see that venerable Gotama.
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth into homelessness, having abandoned a great circle of kinsmen...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth into homelessness, having abandoned vast quantities of gold and silver, both stored in the earth and kept above ground...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth from the home life into homelessness while still young, a youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth and in the prime of his life..."

"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth from the home life into homelessness, shaving off his hair and beard and donning saffron robes, even against the wishes of his weeping parents with tearful faces...

Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring; he is endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, possessing the form of Brahmā, the grace of Brahmā, and is of no mean appearance to look upon...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is virtuous, possessed of noble virtue, possessed of wholesome virtue, and endowed with wholesome virtue..."
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is eloquent, possessed of a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is courteous, distinct, flawless, and capable of making the meaning known...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is a teacher of many teachers...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has exhausted sensual lust and is free from fickleness...
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action, a proponent of performance, one who does not prioritize evil toward the brahmin class...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has gone forth from a high-born family, from an unbroken lineage of kṣatriyas...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has gone forth from a wealthy family, one of great riches and great possessions..."
"Indeed, sirs, people come from across kingdoms and across districts to ask questions of the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, many thousands of deities have gone for refuge with their lives to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, such a fine report concerning the ascetic Gotama has spread abroad:"

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
… [and so on] … “Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
… [and so on] … “Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is one who speaks words of welcome, who is kindly, friendly, free from haughtiness, open-faced, and the first to speak. … [and so on] …
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by the four assemblies...
Indeed, sirs, many gods and humans have placed their confidence in the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, in whatever village or town the ascetic Gotama dwells, non-human beings do not harass the people in that village or town..."
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group; he is reckoned as the foremost among the various founders of sects.
Now, sirs, the fame of the ascetic Gotama has not arisen in the same way as the fame of these other ascetics and brahmins arises, whether by this or that means.
Now, the fame of the ascetic Gotama has arisen on account of his unsurpassed perfection in true knowledge and conduct...

[as before] ...Indeed, sirs, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, together with his sons, his wives, his retinue, and his ministers, has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts to the ascetic Gotama...

[as before] ...Indeed, sirs, King Pasenadi of Kosala, together with his sons, his wives, his retinue, and his ministers, has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts to the ascetic Gotama... [as before].
"Indeed, sir, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, together with his sons, his wife, his retinue, and his ministers, has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha...
Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by King Pasenadi of Kosala..."
"Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by the brahmin Pokkharasāti...
Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama has arrived at Campā and is staying at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond.
Now, sir, whatever ascetics or brahmins come to our village territory, they become our guests."
Furthermore, guests are indeed to be honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by us.
Now, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has arrived at Campā and is staying at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond; the ascetic Gotama is our guest.
And a guest, indeed, is to be honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by us.
"In this respect, that venerable Gotama does not deserve to come to see us;
rather, we ourselves ought to go to see that venerable Gotama.
So much of the venerable Gotama’s praise have I mastered, yet the venerable Gotama is not possessed of praise only to that extent."
“For that venerable Gotama possesses immeasurable beauty.
When this was said, those brahmins said to the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa:

“Since the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa speaks thus in praise of the ascetic Gotama, even if that venerable Gotama were staying a hundred yojanas from here, it would be enough for a faithful son of good family to go to see him, even with a bag of provisions on his back.”
“In that case, sir, let us all go together to visit the ascetic Gotama.
Then the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, accompanied by a great company of brahmins, approached the Gaggarā lotus pond.
Then, as the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa was situated beyond the grove, this reflection arose in his mind:
"If I were to ask the ascetic Gotama a question,
and if the ascetic Gotama were to speak to me thus:"
“Brahmin, this question should not be asked in this way; rather, brahmin, this question should be asked in this way. If I were to say this, this assembly might despise me, thinking:
“The brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is foolish and incompetent; he was unable to ask the ascetic Gotama a question properly.
And whatever assembly might despise one, their reputation would diminish.
Furthermore, for one whose reputation declines, their wealth would also decline.
Our wealth, indeed, was acquired through our reputation.
And if the ascetic Gotama were to question me, and I were not to satisfy his mind with my answer to that question;
And if the ascetic Gotama were to say to me there:
"This question, brahmin, is not to be answered in this way; rather, brahmin, this question is to be answered in such a way," then this assembly would despise me, saying:
"The brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is foolish and incompetent; he was unable to satisfy the mind with his answer to the ascetic Gotama's question."
Furthermore, whatever assembly might despise him, his reputation would diminish.
And for one whose reputation diminishes, their wealth also diminishes;
for our wealth is acquired through reputation.
But if, having come this close, I were to turn back without seeing the ascetic Gotama, this assembly would despise me, saying:
"The brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is foolish, incompetent, arrogant with pride, and afraid; he does not dare to approach the ascetic Gotama for an audience.
How is it that, having come this close, he turns back without seeing the ascetic Gotama?"
"If this assembly were to despise him, his fame would diminish.
And for one whose fame diminishes, their wealth also diminishes;
for our wealth is acquired through fame."
Then the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Some of the brahmin householders from Campā also, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One; having concluded the polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side.
Some, having extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Some, having announced their name and clan, sat down to one side. Some sat down to one side in silence.
There, while sitting and reflecting extensively on this very matter, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa thought:
"What if I were to ask the ascetic Gotama a question?
And if the ascetic Gotama were to speak to me in such a way:"
“Brahmin, this question should not be asked in this way; rather, brahmin, this question should be asked in such a way. For if I were to say this, this assembly might despise me, thinking:
“The brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is foolish and incompetent; he was unable to ask the ascetic Gotama a question properly.
And whatever this assembly might despise, his reputation would diminish.
If one's reputation should decline, their wealth would also decline.
Our wealth, indeed, is acquired through reputation.
Now, if the ascetic Gotama were to question me, and I were not to satisfy his mind with my answer to that question;
And if the ascetic Gotama were to say to me there:
"This question, brahmin, is not to be answered in this way; rather, brahmin, this question is to be answered in that way," then this assembly would despise me, saying:
"The brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is foolish and incompetent; he was unable to satisfy the mind with his answer to the ascetic Gotama's question."
But if this assembly were to despise him, his reputation would diminish.
And for one whose reputation diminishes, their wealth also diminishes;
for our wealth is acquired through reputation.

“Oh, if only the ascetic Gotama would ask me a question regarding my own teacher’s tradition of the Three Vedas! Then I would surely satisfy his mind with my answer to that question. Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, thought this: “Brāhmaṇapaññatti” (The Designation of Brahmins) [The Blessed One then addressed the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa: “Brahmin, do you claim to be a true brahmin? [Soṇadaṇḍa replied: “I do, sir. [The Blessed One asked: “In what way do you claim to be a true brahmin? [Soṇadaṇḍa replied: “Sir, one who is well-born on both sides, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and not reproached in respect of birth, is a true brahmin. [The Blessed One said: “But, brahmin, it is not by mere birth alone that one is a true brahmin. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “How then, sir, is one a true brahmin? [The Blessed One replied: “Brahmin, when one has abandoned the ten qualities of a non-brahmin and possesses the ten qualities of a brahmin, then he is a true brahmin. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “And what, sir, are the ten qualities of a non-brahmin that one has abandoned? [The Blessed One replied: “They are: killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, greed, ill will, and wrong view. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “And what, sir, are the ten qualities of a brahmin that one possesses? [The Blessed One replied: “They are: abstention from killing living beings, abstention from taking what is not given, abstention from sexual misconduct, abstention from false speech, abstention from divisive speech, abstention from harsh speech, abstention from idle chatter, freedom from greed, freedom from ill will, and right view. [The Blessed One continued: “Thus, brahmin, when one has abandoned these ten qualities of a non-brahmin and possesses these ten qualities of a brahmin, then he is a true brahmin. [Soṇadaṇḍa said: “Excellent, sir! Excellent, sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. [The Blessed One said: “But, brahmin, there are four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “What are the four, sir? [The Blessed One replied: “Brahmin, here a certain person seeks his own welfare but not the welfare of others; another seeks the welfare of others but not his own; another seeks neither his own welfare nor the welfare of others; and another seeks both his own welfare and the welfare of others. Among these, the person who seeks both his own welfare and the welfare of others is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent of the four. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “And how, sir, does a person seek both his own welfare and the welfare of others? [The Blessed One replied: “Brahmin, here a certain person himself abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, and from idle chatter; he is without covetousness, without ill will, and holds right view. He encourages others to abstain from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, and from idle chatter; he encourages them to be without covetousness, without ill will, and to hold right view. It is in this way, brahmin, that a person seeks both his own welfare and the welfare of others. [Soṇadaṇḍa said: “Excellent, sir! Excellent, sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned... even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. [The Blessed One said: “Brahmin, there are four kinds of assemblies found existing in the world. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “What are the four, sir? [The Blessed One replied: “Brahmin, here a certain assembly is well-born but not virtuous, wealthy but not learned, eloquent but not wise, and influential but not skilled in counsel. Another assembly is well-born and virtuous, wealthy and learned, eloquent and wise, and influential and skilled in counsel. Among these, the assembly that is well-born and virtuous, wealthy and learned, eloquent and wise, and influential and skilled in counsel is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent of the four. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “And how, sir, is an assembly well-born and virtuous, wealthy and learned, eloquent and wise, and influential and skilled in counsel? [The Blessed One replied: “Brahmin, here a certain assembly consists of those who are well-born on both sides, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and not reproached in respect of birth; they are virtuous, having abandoned the ten qualities of a non-brahmin and possessing the ten qualities of a brahmin; they are wealthy, having acquired great wealth through their own effort and enterprise; they are learned, having mastered the three Vedas with their vocabularies, ritual manuals, phonology, and etymology, and the legends as the fifth, knowing the locations of the verses and the proper pronunciations; they are eloquent, being able to speak on various topics with logic and reasoning; and they are influential and skilled in counsel, being capable of deliberating on matters of state and providing sound advice. It is in this way, brahmin, that an assembly is well-born and virtuous, wealthy and learned, eloquent and wise, and influential and skilled in counsel. [Soṇadaṇḍa said: “Excellent, sir! Excellent, sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned... even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. [The Blessed One said: “Brahmin, there are four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “What are the four, sir? [The Blessed One replied: “Brahmin, here a certain person is a speaker but not a doer; another is a doer but not a speaker; another is neither a speaker nor a doer; and another is both a speaker and a doer. Among these, the person who is both a speaker and a doer is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent of the four. [Soṇadaṇḍa asked: “And how, sir, is a person both a speaker and a doer? [The Blessed One replied: “Brahmin, here a certain person speaks thus: ‘One should refrain from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, and from idle chatter; one should be without covetousness, without ill will, and hold right view. And he himself refrains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, and from idle chatter; he is without covetousness, without ill will, and holds right view. It is in this way, brahmin, that a person is both a speaker and a doer. [Soṇadaṇḍa said: “Excellent, sir! Excellent, sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned... even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in
“This Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is being troubled by his own mind.
Suppose I were to ask the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa a question regarding his own traditional field of the three Vedas.
Then the Blessed One said this to the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa:
“But, brahmin, with how many qualities must a brahmin be endowed for other brahmins to designate him as a brahmin;
and if he says, ‘I am a brahmin,’ would he be speaking rightly and not fall into falsehood?
Then it occurred to the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa:
“Indeed, that which was desired by us, that which was wished for, that which was intended, that which was longed for— ‘Oh,
if only the ascetic Gotama would ask me a question regarding my own teacher’s tradition of the Three Vedas;
then surely I would satisfy his mind with the answer to that question’— therein, the ascetic Gotama [asked me] regarding my own teacher’s tradition.”
“He asks a question concerning the threefold knowledge.
Surely I shall satisfy his mind with my answer to the question.
Then the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, straightening his body and surveying the assembly, said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe five qualities by which one is designated a brahmin;
and if one who says, ‘I am a brahmin,’ speaks correctly, he would not be guilty of falsehood.
What are these five?

"In this case, Master Gotama, a brahmin is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent back through seven generations, unassailable and irreproachable with respect to birth;

he is a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas along with their vocabularies, liturgical formulas, phonology, and etymology, including the histories as the fifth; he is a scholar of the philology and grammar, and is proficient in cosmology and the marks of a Great Man."

He is handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, possessing a divine form and a divine luster, and is of such noble appearance that one never tires of looking at him.
He is virtuous, mature in virtue, and endowed with mature virtue.
He is wise and intelligent, being either the foremost or the second among those who raise the sacrificial ladle.
“Master Gotama, it is on account of these five factors that brahmins designate a man as a brahmin;
one who says ‘I am a brahmin’ may speak correctly and would not be guilty of falsehood.
“But, brahmin, is it possible for brahmins to designate a man as a brahmin on account of four of these five factors, setting aside one factor?”
“Would one speaking thus, ‘I am a brahmin,’ be speaking correctly and not fall into falsehood?
“It is possible, Master Gotama.
For we may set aside the praise of these five factors, Master Gotama.”
For what can mere appearance accomplish?
For, Master Gotama, when a brahmin is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth;

and when he is a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas along with their vocabularies, liturgical formulas, phonology, and etymology, together with the histories as the fifth, a scholar of the prosody and grammar, and one who is not deficient in the Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man—then what can mere appearance accomplish?
He is virtuous, possessing the virtue of the elders and endowed with the virtue of the elders;
he is wise and intelligent, being either the first or the second among those who lift the sacrificial ladle.
It is on account of these four factors, Master Gotama, that brahmins designate someone as a brahmin.
“‘I am a brahmin,’ one who speaks thus would be speaking rightly and would not be guilty of falsehood.
“But, brahmin, is it possible that by setting aside one of these four factors, brahmins could define a person as a brahmin on account of the remaining three factors—
such that one who says, ‘I am a brahmin,’ would be speaking rightly and would not be guilty of falsehood?”
“It is possible, Master Gotama.
For we can set aside the mantras of these four factors.
What indeed will the mantras do?”

For when, Master Gotama, a brahmin is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent back through seven generations, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth;
and he is virtuous, possessing the virtue of the elders and endowed with the virtue of the elders;
and he is wise, intelligent, and foremost or second among those who perform the Soma sacrifice.
“It is by being endowed with these three factors, Master Gotama, that brahmins designate one as a brahmin;
and one who says, ‘I am a brahmin,’ would be speaking correctly and would not be guilty of falsehood.
“But, brahmin, is it possible for brahmins to designate one as a brahmin who is endowed with two of these three factors, setting aside one factor?”
“Could one who says, ‘I am a brahmin,’ speak truthfully and not fall into falsehood?
“It is possible, Master Gotama.
For we would set aside birth among these three factors.”
For what can birth accomplish?
When, Master Gotama, a brahmin is virtuous, possessing the virtue of the elders and endowed with the virtue of the elders;
and when he is wise, intelligent, and foremost or second among those who uphold the sacrificial ladle.
“Master Gotama, it is on account of these two factors that brahmins define one as a brahmin;
and one who says, ‘I am a brahmin,’ would be speaking correctly and would not be guilty of falsehood.
When this was said, those brahmins said this to the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa:
“Do not say that, venerable Soṇadaṇḍa; do not say that, venerable Soṇadaṇḍa.
Venerable Soṇadaṇḍa is indeed disparaging appearance, disparaging the mantras, and disparaging birth; venerable Soṇadaṇḍa is unilaterally leaping into the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama alone.
Then the Blessed One said this to those brahmins:
“If it occurs to you Brahmins thus:
‘The Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is of little learning, the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is of poor speech, the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is of weak wisdom,
and the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is not capable of [engaging] with the ascetic Gotama’— ”
“Let alone the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa; you yourselves should deliberate with me on this statement.
But if it occurs to you brahmins thus:
‘The brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is learned, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is eloquent, and the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is wise…’”
“The brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is capable of conversing with the ascetic Gotama on this matter.
“Then stay back; let the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa converse with me.
When this was said, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa spoke thus to the Blessed One:
“Let Master Gotama remain; let Master Gotama be silent. I myself shall give them a reply in accordance with the Dhamma.
Then the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa said this to those brahmins:
“Sirs, do not speak thus; sirs, do not speak thus:”
“Master Soṇadaṇḍa seems to disparage appearance, he disparages mantras, he disparages birth; Master Soṇadaṇḍa has unilaterally jumped onto the side of the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.
“I do not, sir, disparage appearance, nor mantras, nor birth.
Now at that time, a young brahmin named Aṅgaka, the nephew of the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, was sitting in that assembly.
Then the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa said this to those brahmins:
“Gentlemen, do you see this young man Aṅgaka, our nephew?
“We do, sir.”
“Master, the young man Aṅgaka is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion;
he has the form of Brahmā, the grace of Brahmā, and is no mean sight to behold.
In this assembly, there is no one equal to him in beauty, except for the ascetic Gotama.”

The young brahmin Aṅgaka is a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas along with their vocabularies (nighaṇṭu), liturgical formulas (keṭubha), phonology (sakkharappabheda), and the histories as the fifth; he is a master of exegesis and grammar, and is fully proficient in cosmology and the marks of a Great Man.
I am his teacher of the mantras.
Furthermore, the young brahmin Aṅgaka is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations of ancestors, unblemished and irreproachable by birth.
"I know his mother and father.

The young brahmin Aṅgaka might kill a living being, take what is not given, commit adultery, speak falsehoods, and drink intoxicants; so now, sir, what is the use of appearance, what is the use of mantras, and what is the use of birth?
For when, sir, a brahmin is virtuous, possessed of the virtue of the elders, and endowed with the virtue of the elders..."
"He is wise and intelligent, being either the first or the second among those who hold up the sacrificial ladle.
It is on account of these two factors, sir, that brahmins designate one as a brahmin;
and one who says 'I am a brahmin' would be speaking correctly and would not be guilty of falsehood."
6. Discussion on Virtue and Wisdom:
“But, brahmin, is it possible for the brahmins, by setting aside one of these two factors and being endowed with only the other, to designate someone as a brahmin;
such that one who says, ‘I am a brahmin,’ would be speaking correctly and would not be guilty of falsehood?”
“No indeed, Master Gotama.
For wisdom, Master Gotama, is purified by virtue; virtue is purified by wisdom.
Where there is virtue, there is wisdom; where there is wisdom, there is virtue.”
For one who possesses virtue there is wisdom, and for one who possesses wisdom there is virtue.
Indeed, virtue and wisdom together are declared to be the highest in the world.
Just as, Master Gotama, one might wash hand with hand, or foot with foot;
In the same way, Master Gotama, wisdom is purified by virtue, and virtue is purified by wisdom.
Where there is virtue, there is wisdom; where there is wisdom, there is virtue.
For one who possesses virtue, there is wisdom; for one who possesses wisdom, there is virtue.
“Moreover, in this world, virtue and wisdom are declared to be supreme.
“So it is, brahmin; so it is, brahmin. For, brahmin, wisdom is purified by virtue, and virtue is purified by wisdom.
Where there is virtue, there is wisdom; where there is wisdom, there is virtue.”
For one who possesses virtue there is wisdom, and for one who possesses wisdom there is virtue.
Indeed, virtue and wisdom together are declared to be the highest in the world.
Just as, brahmin, one might wash hand with hand or foot with foot;
In the same way, brahmin, wisdom is purified by virtue, and virtue is purified by wisdom.
Where there is virtue, there is wisdom; where there is wisdom, there is virtue.
For one who possesses virtue, there is wisdom; for one who possesses wisdom, there is virtue.
“Furthermore, in this world, virtue and wisdom are declared to be supreme.
But what, brahmin, is that virtue?
And what is that wisdom?”
“We have reached the limit of our knowledge regarding this matter, Master Gotama.
It would be well if Master Gotama himself would explain the meaning of these words.
“In that case, brahmin, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this world, brahmin, a Tathāgata arises, an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha... [as before] ...”
In this way, brahmin, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue.
This, brahmin, is that virtue … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna … [and so on] … pe …
He directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge and vision [of liberation]...
This too is his wisdom...
he understands: "There is nothing further beyond this state of being."
"This too belongs to his wisdom;
this indeed, brahmin, is that wisdom.
7. Soṇadaṇḍa’s Declaration of Laymanship.
When this was said, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or might show the way, or might hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama.
I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
And may Master Gotama, together with the community of monks, consent to accept a meal from me tomorrow.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, when that night had passed, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared in his own residence and had the time announced to the Blessed One:
"It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready."

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and together with the community of monks, approached the residence of the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, with his own hands, personally served and satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods.
Then the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, if I were to rise from my seat while present in this assembly and pay homage to Master Gotama, that assembly would despise me.”
Moreover, whatever assembly might despise him, his fame would diminish.
And for one whose fame diminishes, his wealth would also diminish;
for our wealth is acquired through fame.
"Moreover, Master Gotama, if I were to go into an assembly and raise my joined palms, may Master Gotama accept that as my rising from my seat for him.
And if, Master Gotama, I were to go into an assembly and remove my turban, may Master Gotama accept that as my prostration with my head at his feet.
Furthermore, Master Gotama, if I were to go in a vehicle and, having descended from the vehicle, were to pay homage to Master Gotama, that assembly might despise me."
Furthermore, whatever assembly might despise him, his reputation would diminish; and for one whose reputation diminishes, his wealth also diminishes.
Now, our wealth is acquired through reputation.
Moreover, Master Gotama, if I were to raise my goad-stick while seated in a carriage, may the venerable Gotama accept that I descend from the carriage.
“Moreover, Master Gotama, if while riding in my carriage I were to remove my parasol, may the Blessed Gotama accept this as a salutation from my head.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
The Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, the fourth, is finished.
